description: A team that is part of something better
summary:
ORBITFORGE is a 3D space-mission game built in Unreal Engine 5 for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players begin as a newly selected astronaut at a space-agency headquarters. In Mission 1 they assemble a rocket. Mission 2 is the launch and orbit plan, set against real weather and wind. In Mission 3 they live aboard a spacecraft on a multi-day journey to Mars. Mission 4 covers landing and surface research, and Mission 5 is the return home. Each mission combines exploration with 12 interactive mini-games: visual calibration, timeline repair, zero-gravity survival, orbit-angle and trajectory control, orbital burns, signal recovery, crew health management, wire repair, precision landing, rover exploration and a final call home.

The game runs on a two-currency economy. Players earn Dollars from mission and mini-game performance, then spend them on 26 rocket, robot and suit modules. They use Repair Tokens to fix random spacecraft alerts.

A science track lets players design an Earth-observation CubeSat end to end, from payload and power to orbit, launch and operations. It uses real optics, orbital mechanics and comparisons with NASA missions such as Landsat, MODIS, ECOSTRESS and GEDI. The game teaches how real missions are designed, flown and kept alive.
details:
What it does: ORBITFORGE turns mission design into something you play. You walk a space-agency headquarters in first person, talk to the team and complete five connected missions:
1. Assemble the Rocket: inspect the rocket and train on three mini-games (AstroSight visual calibration, ChronoSync timeline repair, Astro Anti-Gravity zero-g survival). Buy parts in the Mission Store, install them in the right sockets and pass the final inspection.
2. Launch and Orbit Plan: pick a launch date, analyse weather, wind, visibility, ceiling and lightning risk, and set the ascent trajectory. Plan orbits and escape boosts with the Orbit Angle Controller and Orbital Trajectory mini-games, then launch.
3. Space Journey: live in a six-room spacecraft (crew cabin, flight control, communication, engineering bay, research storage, corridor). Each day brings an orbital blast burn, signal recovery with mission control and a Human Performance Monitor for stamina and mental health. Random alerts (micro-meteoroids, power surges, oxygen leaks) are fixed with a Repair Token, an emergency Dollar repair, or by accepting the damage.
4. Landing and Research: choose a landing zone and fly the precision landing. Deploy the rover, then collect, store and analyse a Mars soil sample.
5. Return: plant a personal flag, run the return checklist, plan the return trajectory and fly home.
Economy: two currencies, Dollars and Repair Tokens. Mini-games pay by performance band (Failed, Basic, Good, Excellent, Perfect). Missions pay completion bonuses and Repair Tokens. Completing a mission unlocks products in a 26-module catalogue (tanks, boosters, orbiters, engines, wings, launch pads, radar, robots, suits), which are then bought with Dollars. All prices and stats are illustrative game-balancing values.
Science track (FORESTWATCH): design an Earth-observation CubeSat that watches a drought-stricken forest. The chain runs objective, wavelength, instrument, optics, followed by a live mass, power, link and thermal budget. Then plan the orbit, simulate the launch, operate the spacecraft for a year and compare your results with real NASA missions (Landsat, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GEDI).
Benefits and impact: players learn the real trade-offs of spaceflight (mass versus thrust, weather limits, fuel budgets, crew wellbeing, damage control, science return) with immediate, explained feedback. It works for students and for anyone curious about how missions are designed and kept alive.
Tools and languages: Unreal Engine 5.8 (C++), an engine-independent deterministic C++17 simulation core with automated tests, 17 HTML/CSS/JavaScript mini-game activities in a validated in-game host (Mission 1 and 2 games also native Slate UI), Python tooling for asset import and testing, and 3D models converted with trimesh.
Creativity: every number in the game comes from a rule the player can see and learn from. The spacecraft interior and headquarters were redesigned from the team's own reference concepts, and the economy ties performance, risk and progression together without any extra currency.
Use of SI: code, tests, tooling and documentation were written with the help of an SI coding assistant (Anthropic's Claude, in Claude Code), directed, reviewed and tested by the team. The game concept, design and mini-game designs are the team's own. No NASA logos or insignia are used.
